title: Fraunhofer Diffraction
short_intro: Fraunhofer diffraction is a phenomenon of light bending around obstacles or apertures where both the source of light and the observation screen are effectively at an infinite distance from the aperture. Under these conditions, the wavefronts incident on the aperture and diffracted from it are planar.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of single-slit diffraction patterns, central maxima, secondary maxima and minima conditions, and relation with wavelength and slit width.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous mathematical treatment of single-slit and double-slit Fraunhofer diffraction, intensity distribution, angular width of central maxima, and diffraction grating spectra.

prerequisites: Superposition of waves and phasor addition

concept_notes.heading: Condition for Fraunhofer Diffraction
bullets: The source of light and the screen are at infinite distances from the diffracting aperture, achieved practically using two convex lenses.
The incident wavefronts on the obstacle or aperture are planar.
The diffracted rays arriving at any point on the screen are parallel to each other.

concept_notes.heading: Single-Slit Intensity Distribution
bullets: The diffraction pattern consists of a central bright maximum flanked by alternate secondary minima and weaker secondary maxima.
The angular half-width of the central maximum is given by sin(θ) = λ/a, where a is the slit width.
Most of the incident light energy is concentrated within the central maximum.

concept_notes.heading: Minima and Secondary Maxima Conditions
bullets: Minima are formed when the path difference between light rays originating from the extreme edges of the slit is an integral multiple of wavelength (λ).
Secondary maxima are approximately located midway between the secondary minima, where the path difference is odd multiples of λ/2.
As the slit width a increases, the central maximum becomes narrower and more intense.

concept_notes.heading: Comparison with Fresnel Diffraction
bullets: In Fresnel diffraction, either the source, the screen, or both are at finite distances from the aperture, requiring spherical or cylindrical wavefront analysis.
Fraunhofer diffraction is a special limiting case of Fresnel diffraction where wavefront curvature is negligible.
Fraunhofer diffraction is mathematically simpler to handle using rectilinear propagation approximations and Fourier transforms.

derivations.title: Fraunhofer Diffraction at a Single Slit
derivations.conditions: Normal incidence of plane wavefront of wavelength λ on a slit of width a, observation on a focal plane screen.
steps: Divide the slit of width a into n equal infinitesimal strips. The path difference between consecutive strips for a diffraction angle θ is dx sin(θ).
The phase difference between consecutive strips is dφ = (2π/λ) dx sin(θ). Integrating across the slit width from -a/2 to a/2 gives the resultant amplitude R = A₀ (sin α)/α, where α = (π a sin θ)/λ.
The intensity I is proportional to R², yielding I = I₀ (sin α / α)².

derivations.title: Positions of Minima for Single Slit
derivations.conditions: Intensity vanishing condition in single-slit diffraction.
steps: Minima occur when the amplitude factor sin α = 0, provided α ≠ 0.
Substituting α gives (π a sin\theta)/λ = mπ, leading to a sin θ = mλ.
derivations.result: a sin\theta = mlambda quad (m = pm 1, pm 2, pm 3, ...)

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity vs Phase Parameter (α) for Single Slit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A symmetrical curve showing a high central peak at α = 0 with decreasing secondary peaks at α ≈ ±1.43π, ±2.46π, with intensity vanishing at α = ±π, ±2π, ...
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how diffracted intensity drops rapidly away from the center, concentrating about 90% of energy in the central maximum.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in PGT to identify positions of secondary maxima and minima.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Formation of Fraunhofer Diffraction using Convex Lenses
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A point or slit source at the focus of lens L₁, parallel beam falling on aperture, and lens L₂ focusing parallel diffracted rays onto a screen.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the experimental realization of infinite source and screen distances in a laboratory setup.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: TGT conceptual questions regarding the necessity and placement of lenses.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Grating Diffraction Spectrum
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Sharp principal maxima peaks separated by broad regions of darkness and faint subsidiary maxima.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the sharp dispersive power of diffraction gratings compared to double slits.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: PGT numericals and conceptual questions on resolving power and missing orders.

solved_numericals.question: Light of wavelength 500 nm falls normally on a single slit of width 0.2 mm. Calculate the angular position of the first secondary minimum.
solution_steps: Identify given values: lambda = 500 nm = 5 \times 10^{-7} m, a = 0.2 mm = 2 \times 10^{-4} m, m = 1.
Use the minima condition: a sin\theta = mlambda.
Since sin\theta is very small, \theta approx 2.5 \times 10^{-3} radians.

solved_numericals.question: A slit of width 0.5 mm is illuminated normally with light of wavelength 589 nm. Find the linear width of the central maximum on a screen placed 1.0 m away from the lens.
solution_steps: Identify given values: a = 0.5 mm = 5 \times 10^{-4} m, lambda = 589 nm = 5.89 \times 10^{-7} m, f = 1.0 m.
Linear width of central maximum is given by \beta = (2 f lambda) / a.

solved_numericals.question: Find the maximum number of orders visible when light of wavelength 600 nm is normally incident on a diffraction grating having 500 lines per mm.
solution_steps: Find grating element (a + b): 1 mm / 500 = 2 \times 10^{-6} m.
Use grating formula for maximum order: (a + b) sin\theta = nlambda. For maximum order, set sin\theta = 1.
Since order must be an integer, round down to the nearest integer.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes scalar wave theory, ignoring polarization effects of light waves.
Valid strictly when the distance of source and screen from the aperture are large compared to the size of the aperture.

common_misconceptions.correct: Fraunhofer diffraction involves plane wavefronts incident and diffracted.
common_misconceptions.why: Wavefront curvature is assumed negligible due to infinite distance.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The central maximum in single-slit diffraction has the same width as secondary maxima.
common_misconceptions.correct: The central maximum has double the width of any secondary maximum.
common_misconceptions.why: The central maximum spans from m = -1 to m = +1, occupying an angular range of 2lambda/a.

quick_revision: Central maximum width is 2lambda/a in angular terms and 2flambda/a in linear terms for a single slit.
Phase Parameter alpha: alpha = \frac{pi a sin\theta}{lambda}
Intensity Distribution for Single Slit: I = I_0 left(\frac{sinalpha}{alpha}\right)^2
